subQuestions.label: 1(b)
subQuestions.questionText: Show that the equation $x^2 - 2px = -p^2$ has equal roots for all values of $p$.
subQuestions.memoText:
$x^2 - 2px + p^2 = 0$
$\Delta = (-2p)^2 - 4(1)(p^2) = 4p^2 - 4p^2 = 0$ for all $p$, so the roots are equal.
(Alternatively $(x - p)(x - p) = 0 \Rightarrow x = p$.)

subQuestions.label: 2(d)
subQuestions.questionText: If $\log x + \log z = \log y^2$, show that $x$, $y$ and $z$ form a geometric sequence.
subQuestions.memoText:
$\log xz = \log y^2$
$xz = y^2$
So $\dfrac{y}{x} = \dfrac{z}{y}$, i.e. the terms have a common ratio — they form a geometric sequence.

$x = \pm 2$

questions.title: Quadratic Number Pattern & a Sigma Sum

subQuestions.label: 7(a)
subQuestions.questionText: The first four terms of a quadratic number pattern are $4$, $7$, $x + 7$ and $x + y + 7$. If the fourth term is 58, determine the values of $x$ and $y$.
subQuestions.memoText:
$x + y + 7 = 58 \Rightarrow x + y = 51$.
First differences: $3$, $x$, $51 - x$. Second differences: $x - 3$ and $51 - 2x$, which must be equal:
$x - 3 = 51 - 2x$
$3x = 54$
$x = 18$
$y = 51 - 18 = 33$

questions.title: Parabola & Hyperbola with Axes of Symmetry

subQuestions.label: 9(a)
subQuestions.questionText:
In the diagram $f(x) = a(x - m)^2 + k$ and $h(x) = \dfrac{1}{x - p} + q$. The equations of the axes of symmetry of $h$ are $y = -x + 2$ and $y = x + 6$. D is the turning point of $f$ and lies on both axes of symmetry of $h$. C is a point of intersection of $h$ and the axis of symmetry $y = x + 6$. A and B are $x$-intercepts (of the axes of symmetry). The graph of $f$ passes through the origin.

Determine the domain of $h$.
subQuestions.memoText:
The asymptotes meet where the axes of symmetry meet: $-x + 2 = x + 6 \Rightarrow -2x = 4 \Rightarrow x = -2$, so $p = -2$.
Domain: $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $x \neq -2$

subQuestions.label: 9(b)
subQuestions.questionText: Determine the values of $a$, $m$ and $k$.
subQuestions.memoText:
D is the intersection of the axes of symmetry: $x = -2$, $y = -(-2) + 2 = 4$, so $D(-2; 4)$.
D is the turning point of $f$, so $m = -2$ and $k = 4$.
$f$ passes through the origin: $0 = a(0 + 2)^2 + 4 \Rightarrow 0 = 4a + 4 \Rightarrow a = -1$.

subQuestions.label: 10(a)(1)
subQuestions.questionText: If $g(x) = -a^{-x} + k$ then determine the coordinates of the $x$-intercept of the graph of $g$ in terms of $a$ and $k$.
subQuestions.memoText:
$0 = -a^{-x} + k$
$k = a^{-x}$
$-x = \log_a k$
$x = -\log_a k$, so the $x$-intercept is $(-\log_a k; 0)$.

subQuestions.label: 10(a)(2)
subQuestions.questionText: Sketch the graph of $y = g(x)$ if $0 < a < 1$ and $k > 2$.
subQuestions.memoText:
$g(x) = -a^{-x} + k$. Since $0 < a < 1$, $a^{-x}$ increases as $x$ increases, so $g$ is decreasing.
Horizontal asymptote $y = k$ (with $k > 2$); the curve approaches $y = k$ from below as $x \to -\infty$ and decreases steeply for large $x$.
$x$-intercept: $(-\log_a k; 0)$; $y$-intercept: $(0; k - 1)$.
Marks: asymptote; shape; intercept.

questions.title: Optimisation — Minimum Surface Area of a Can

subQuestions.questionText:
A local food packaging company produces canned food in the shape of cylinders, each with a fixed volume of $150\pi$ cm$^3$. To reduce production costs, the company aims to minimise the total surface area of each can.

Given that $r$ represents the radius and $h$ the can's height, determine the radius which will result in minimum surface area.

Useful formulae: $S = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi rh$ and $V = \pi r^2 h$.
subQuestions.memoText:
$\pi r^2 h = 150\pi \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{150}{r^2}$
$S = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r\left(\dfrac{150}{r^2}\right) = 2\pi r^2 + \dfrac{300\pi}{r}$
$\dfrac{dS}{dr} = 4\pi r - 300\pi r^{-2}$
$4\pi r - 300\pi r^{-2} = 0$
$4r^3 = 300$
$r^3 = 75$
$r = \sqrt[3]{75}$

subQuestions.memoText:
$P(H \text{ and } G) = \dfrac{5}{21}$
$P(H) \times P(G) = \dfrac{11}{21} \times \dfrac{7}{21}$
$P(H \text{ and } G) \neq P(H) \times P(G)$
The events are NOT independent.

subQuestions.label: 13(c)
subQuestions.questionText:
Given that A and B are two events in a sample space S, with $n(S) = 10$ and $n(A) = 9$, and $P(B') = 0{,}2$.

Masego argues that the probability of A and B is at least 70%. Do you agree with this claim? Justify your answer with reasoning and calculations.
subQuestions.memoText:
$P(A) = \dfrac{9}{10} = 0{,}9$ and $P(B) = 1 - 0{,}2 = 0{,}8$.
$P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ or } B) = 0{,}9 + 0{,}8 - P(A \text{ or } B) = 1{,}7 - P(A \text{ or } B)$.
Since $0 \leq P(A \text{ or } B) \leq 1$: $P(A \text{ and } B) \geq 1{,}7 - 1 = 0{,}7$.
Masego's claim is correct.
